researched_by: the council's own car park pages and tariff table, its parking policy, the June 2025 Cabinet car park review, and motorhome-community reports corroborating the rules and locations on the ground
policy_summary:
The most permissive council regime found in the dataset so far, and it is permissive by written policy rather than by neglect. Powys's parking policy states plainly: 'Motorhomes and caravans are permitted to use most long stay car parks. Where they are permitted it will be allowed for that vehicle to be used for camping purposes for 1 night in any 7 day period.' That is an explicit right to SLEEP, not merely to park - the opposite of the Ceredigion, Gwynedd and Anglesey position, where sleeping is confined to designated bays or banned outright.

The money side matches. Charging runs 08:00-18:00 only and the published tariff table carries an explicit 'Overnight: GBP0.00' line for every class, including the larger-vehicle class that covers motorhomes, goods vehicles over 3t and car-plus-caravan. Daytime for a motorhome is GBP3.00 for an hour rising to GBP10.00 for over four hours (roughly double the car rate) under the tariffs that took effect on 1 August 2025. Arrive after 18:00 and leave before 08:00 and you pay nothing at all.

Access is controlled by vehicle class per car park rather than by an overnight rule. Each car park is designated for 'all vehicle types', for 'motorcars/motorhomes with trailers', or for 'motorcars and motorcycles only'; motorhomes are lawfully in the first two and not the third. Fifteen or so long-stay car parks across the county fall in the permissive classes, which effectively gives Powys a free, unbranded aire network covering Welshpool, Newtown, Machynlleth, Llanidloes, Llandrindod Wells, Builth Wells, Brecon, Hay-on-Wye and Crickhowell - the whole spine of Mid Wales.

The direction of travel is to keep it. The June 2025 Cabinet car park review recorded that 'the current absence of night-time charging is an area where Powys is often complimented, giving the opportunity for tourers, lorry drivers, guests, and residents the opportunity to park up overnight (6pm to 8am) for free', and concluded that introducing night-time charging would need extra enforcement and was 'not considered viable at this current time'. That was written against a GBP9.6m budget gap, so the decision was taken with every incentive to go the other way. The only motorhome-hostile idea in the review papers - a consultant's suggestion that 'under-used car parks on the outskirts of towns could be used to discourage people from coming into town with large vehicles' - was not carried into any recommendation.

On the Welsh aires question: Powys has no Arosfan-style scheme, no trial and no stated refusal to run one. It has never needed the format. Gwynedd charges GBP16.50 for 16:00-10:00 in a designated bay; Powys gives you 18:00-08:00 free in an ordinary long-stay car park and lets you sleep there once a week.

Two big draws inside the county boundary are NOT the council's and are covered by separate register entries: the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority runs its own car parks across the south of the county, and the Elan Valley estate above Rhayader belongs to Dwr Cymru Welsh Water. Nothing in this file applies to either. Every car park listed here is a Powys County Council pay-and-display car park in a town.
notes:
This is the strongest counter-example in the dataset to the claim that a council must build aires to stop unmanaged overnighting. Powys did nothing structural: it simply never wrote a sleeping ban into its policy, never charged at night, and designates enough car parks for large vehicles that vans have somewhere obvious to go. The result is a de facto network with no capital cost, no branding and no press releases - and, notably, no recurring 'motorhome nuisance' news story of the kind that has followed Aberystwyth since 2013 and Anglesey since 2024.

The one-night-in-seven limit is the load-bearing detail and it is real, not theoretical: motorhome forum posts and park4night entries for Welshpool quote it back verbatim, which means it is on the signs. It is also what keeps the arrangement politically survivable - it permits touring and forbids residence.

Caveat on the policy's status. The wording quoted above is from the version that went to Cabinet as a draft in September 2017; the council publishes the adopted successor as 'Parking Policy 2018' (version 1, 9 January 2018) but that PDF is not machine-retrievable. The substance is corroborated by current practice, current tariffs and current user reports, so the risk is that the exact numbers have drifted, not that the permission has been withdrawn.

Geography matters more here than anywhere else in the dataset. Powys is the largest Welsh county by area and the permissive car parks are all in towns strung along the A483, A470, A44 and A40. The Cambrian Mountains, the Elan Valley approaches and the upland lanes have no council provision at all, and nothing found suggests the council has ever made a lay-by order - the pressure that produced Gwynedd's unpublished lay-by orders does not appear to exist here.
open_questions: Text of the Powys County Council (Off-Street Parking Places) Order 2022 (PP062). The order sets the vehicle classes and would confirm whether it contains a sleeping or camping clause at all; the Traffic Penalty Tribunal copy is blocked to automated retrieval.
Whether the adopted Parking Policy 2018 still carries the 'camping purposes for 1 night in any 7 day period' wording unchanged. Only the September 2017 draft could be read.

How the one-night-in-seven limit is actually enforced - there is no ANPR and charging staff are off duty overnight, so in practice it looks like signage plus civil enforcement officers recognising repeat vehicles.

Vehicle classes for Rhayader (Dark Lane), Knighton (Bowling Green Lane) and Llanidloes (Mount Street). The council's pages give the car parks as long stay but do not state which vehicles are permitted.

Whether motorhomes may use the Brecon Coach and Lorry Park overnight at the GBP10 coach/lorry day rate or free after 18:00 like other classes - the council calls it suitable for motorhomes but tariffs it separately.

Bay counts. Powys publishes none, and capacity for large vehicles in these car parks is the practical limit on the whole arrangement - motorhome reports suggest roughly ten vans at Brecon Promenade and ten spaces at Welshpool.

sites.name: Promenade Car Park, Brecon
sites.search_hint: Promenade car park, Brecon, alongside the River Usk
sites.notes: Long stay, designated for ALL VEHICLE TYPES - the only Brecon car park that is. Free between 18:00 and 08:00; sleeping in the vehicle permitted one night in any seven under the council's parking policy. Daytime is the larger-vehicle tariff, GBP3.00 for an hour to GBP10.00 for over four hours. Alongside the Usk on the western edge of town, a short riverside walk into the centre. Motorhome reports put realistic capacity at about ten vans. The council also lists Upper and Lower Promenade separately on its season ticket page.
sites.geocode_precision: riverside car park off the Promenade, GPS from a motorhome stopover listing

sites.name: Berriew Street Car Park, Welshpool
sites.notes: Long stay, all vehicle types. The best-documented Powys stopover: motorhome listings quote the rule back as 'free 6pm to 8am' and '1 nite in 7', which means it is on the signage. Roughly ten usable spaces, sloping. Town centre, walkable to Powis Castle. Users note you must return to the machine at 08:00 if you intend to stay into the morning.
sites.geocode_precision: GPS from a motorhome stopover listing, agrees with the council's Berriew Street address

sites.name: Church Street Car Park, Welshpool
sites.notes: Long stay, all vehicle types. The second of Welshpool's two permissive car parks; the park4night entry filed under Oldford Lane, which adjoins, reports the same free 18:00-08:00 window and one-night-in-seven rule with some weekend noise from the town centre.

sites.name: Oxford Road Car Park, Hay-on-Wye
sites.notes: Long stay, all vehicle types - the only one of Hay's three car parks that admits motorhomes; Market Square is short stay cars only and Motte and Bailey is cars and motorcycles only. Named by motorhome users as a regular Powys stop but reported as noisy with early morning traffic. Inside the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park boundary but a Powys County Council car park, not a national park one.

sites.notes: Machynlleth's only pay and display car park, long stay, all vehicle types. sites.name: Dark Lane Car Park, Rhayader
sites.notes: Rhayader's only council car park, long stay - but the council page states no vehicle class, so whether motorhomes are within the designation is unconfirmed. Recorded because Rhayader is the gateway to the Elan Valley, which is Dwr Cymru Welsh Water land with its own rules and is NOT covered by anything in this file. If Dark Lane does admit motorhomes it is the only lawful free overnight stop for that whole valley.

sites.name: Powys car parks designated for motorcars and motorcycles only
sites.notes: Powys controls motorhome access by vehicle class per car park rather than by an overnight rule, so the restriction is simply the list of car parks a motorhome is not designated to use: Brecon - George Street, Inner Viaduct, Y Gaer, Alexandra Road, Outer Viaduct, Kensington, Dinas Road, Scout Lane and Canal Road; Llandrindod Wells - Town Hall and Middleton Street; Hay-on-Wye - Market Square and Motte and Bailey; Presteigne - Hereford Street and High Street; Ystradgynlais - Heol Eglwys and Heol Maes-y-Dre; Welshpool - The Seven Stars; Newtown - Gas Street; Knighton - Norton Arms. Ystradgynlais and Presteigne have NO motorhome-designated council car park at all. No pin: this is an estate-wide class designation, not a place.
